What should you know before selling a house in Phoenix, AZ?

Phoenix is the largest city in Arizona and the county seat of Maricopa County, so a house sale here involves the city, the county recorder and the county treasurer in the same transaction. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 1,665,481 residents, and the city covers about 518 square miles of land.

This page explains how the city is divided into villages, what the heat does to a house, how school districts overlap, the city's short-term rental permit, the deed steps in downtown Phoenix and the property tax dates.

How is the city of Phoenix divided into villages?

Phoenix is divided into 15 urban villages, and each has a Village Planning Committee appointed by the mayor and City Council. The villages are Ahwatukee Foothills, Alhambra, Camelback East, Central City, Deer Valley, Desert View, Encanto, Estrella, Laveen, Maryvale, North Gateway, North Mountain, Paradise Valley, Rio Vista and South Mountain.

The committees hear rezoning cases, general plan amendments and text amendments, then pass a recommendation to the Planning Commission and the City Council. That matters if a buyer plans to change the use of your lot, because the case will pass through the village committee first.

Wikipedia traces the village model to the 1970s, when the Phoenix Concept 2000 plan split the city into nine original villages, each with a core where greater height and density were allowed. South Mountain separates Ahwatukee from the rest of the city, and Camelback Mountain, North Mountain, Sunnyslope Mountain and Piestewa Peak stand inside the developed area.

How did Phoenix grow into the largest city in Arizona?

Phoenix began as an agricultural community in 1867 and is now the fifth most populous city in the United States. It was incorporated on February 25, 1881, and became the capital of the Arizona Territory in 1889. Its canal system supported farming, and the "Five C's" of cotton, cattle, citrus, climate and copper anchored its early economy until after World War II, when high-tech companies moved in and air conditioning made the summers easier to live with.

Sun City, which opened in 1960, became a template for retirement communities. The housing market later fell hard in the subprime crisis: by early 2009 the median home price was about $150,000, down from a peak of $262,000 in 2007, according to Wikipedia.

What does extreme heat mean for a Phoenix house?

Phoenix has a hot desert climate, and buyers and inspectors treat the air conditioner and roof as major items. The city sees about 111 days a year with a high of at least 100 degrees, and highs reach 110 degrees on average 21 days a year. The record high is 122 degrees, set June 26, 1990.

Recent summers have been far above average. July 2023 averaged 102.7 degrees, with a streak of 31 days at 110 or higher, and 2024 brought 113 straight days of 100 degrees or more and a record 70 days at 110 or higher. The urban heat island also keeps nights warm: the daily normal low stays at or above 80 degrees for an average of 74 days each summer. Wikipedia notes that nearly all Phoenix homes have air conditioning.

Before listing, gather:

  • Service dates and invoices for each cooling unit.
  • The age of the roof and any repairs.
  • Records of shade, insulation or window work done to cut cooling costs.

Which school districts serve a Phoenix address?

A Phoenix address can fall in any of 33 school districts, because annexations over the years pulled many pre-existing districts inside the city limits. Twenty-one elementary districts, four high school districts and four unified districts cover the city, and well over 100 charter schools operate in it.

The Phoenix Union High School District, with more than 27,000 students and 16 schools, is one of the largest in the country. Glendale Union, Tempe Union and Tolleson Union serve only parts of Phoenix, and of the four unified districts only Paradise Valley covers Phoenix completely. Because the boundaries are tangled, confirm the district for the exact address with the district office before you describe a school zone.

Do Phoenix short-term rental permit rules affect a sale?

They do if the house has been rented short term, because Phoenix now requires a permit, not a registration. The change took effect November 6, 2023, after Arizona Senate Bill 1168 let cities set up a limited permit process. The city must issue or deny a permit within 7 days of receiving a complete application.

  • The initial and renewal fee is $250 per permit, and applications go through the SHAPE PHX portal.
  • The owner needs an Arizona Transaction Privilege Tax license and must update the rental status with the Maricopa County Assessor.
  • A Notice of Intent goes by certified mail to adjacent neighbors and to registered homeowners associations and neighborhood associations within 600 feet.
  • Court-adjudicated violations carry minimum penalties of $500, $1,000 and $3,500, and a permit can be suspended for 12 months after three violations in a year.
  • For a property with an accessory dwelling unit that received a certificate of occupancy on or after September 14, 2024, an owner who applies on or after April 4, 2026 must file a notarized attestation that the owner will live on the property.

Contact the city's short-term rental staff at vacation.rental@phoenix.gov or 602-534-9723 for the status of a particular permit.

How is a Phoenix sale recorded and taxed?

The deed is filed at the Maricopa County Recorder, 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200, which is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. and takes in-person filings without an appointment. A deed needs an Affidavit of Property Value or an exemption code, and the standard fee is $30.00 per document. A.R.S. 11-1133 requires the buyer and seller to certify the price, parcel number and sale date.

Property tax follows A.R.S. 42-18052: half is due October 1 and half March 1, the first half is delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and the second after 5:00 p.m. on May 1, and a bill of $100 or less is due October 1 and delinquent after December 31. The Maricopa County Treasurer publishes the same dates. November 1 has passed, so ask the treasurer or your title company whether the first half on your parcel has been paid.

How do people get around Phoenix?

Phoenix is organized on a flat street grid, and the freeway system ties its villages together. Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport serves more than 100 cities with nonstop flights, Phoenix-Mesa Gateway Airport in Mesa handles additional commercial traffic, and Valley Metro operates a 38.5 mile light rail system with an A Line and a B Line. Wikipedia reports that 3.38 percent of workers commute by public transit.

Where the house sits relative to a rail stop or a freeway on-ramp is a fair point to mention in a listing.

Yes. Phoenix requires a short-term rental permit from the Planning and Development Department, with a $250 initial and renewal fee. The owner also needs an Arizona Transaction Privilege Tax license and must notify neighbors by certified mail.

Phoenix has 15 urban villages, from Ahwatukee Foothills to South Mountain. Each has a Village Planning Committee that reviews rezoning cases before they reach the Planning Commission.

How do I sell my house fast in Tucson, AZ?

Choose between listing with an agent, selling on your own, or taking an as-is cash offer, then plan the closing in Pima County. Whichever you pick, the house ends up with an escrow at a title company, a deed recorded by the Pima County Recorder and a sales affidavit attached to that deed.

A traditional listing suits a house in good repair that can wait for a buyer's loan to fund. A cash sale suits a house with deferred repairs, a tenant, a probate wrinkle or a tax bill you want settled quickly. The city covers a large desert basin, so a house can have little in common with one a few miles away.

Gather these before you ask for offers:

  • Lender payoff letters and the Pima County Assessor parcel number.
  • Any permit paperwork for casitas, room additions, pool work or replaced HVAC and water heaters.
  • Utility status, since a house with power or gas off for months needs a reconnect permit.
  • Your current Pima County Treasurer tax statement.

What do the numbers say about Tucson homes?

Tucson is the second-largest city in Arizona. The Census Bureau estimates 548,371 residents on July 1, 2025, up from 542,629 at the 2020 census, spread over 240.99 square miles of land.

About 16.2% of residents are 65 or older and the mean commute is 21.9 minutes. Those are citywide figures. A midtown house near the University of Arizona and a foothills property can sit far apart on price, so compare recent sales on your own street.

What is Tucson like, and which neighborhoods matter to buyers?

Tucson sits on an alluvial plain in the Sonoran Desert, ringed by the Santa Catalina and Tortolita Mountains to the north, the Santa Ritas to the south, the Rincons to the east and the Tucson Mountains to the west. It is the Pima County seat and the largest city in southern Arizona.

The Spanish built the Presidio San Agustin del Tucson in 1775, the United States acquired the region in the 1853 Gadsden Purchase, and Tucson was the Arizona Territory capital from 1867 to 1877. The street grid centers on Stone Avenue and Broadway Boulevard. The Tucson Mountains blocked growth to the west, so the city spread east.

Older neighborhoods near downtown show up often in listings:

  • El Presidio, the oldest, and Barrio Historico, also called Barrio Libre.
  • Armory Park, directly south of downtown, and Barrio Anita beside Interstate 10.
  • Sam Hughes, east of the university, and Feldman's, just north and northwest of it.
  • West University, Menlo Park below Sentinel Peak, and the Fourth Avenue district.

Interstate 10 runs through the city toward Phoenix and Las Cruces, and Interstate 19 runs south to Nogales. Suburbs and neighbors include Oro Valley, Marana, Sahuarita, South Tucson and the Catalina Foothills. The University of Arizona is the city's largest employer at 10,864 employees, followed by RTX and Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, according to the city's 2023 financial report.

How do Tucson's heat and monsoon storms affect a house?

Summer heat and monsoon rain both leave marks that a buyer's inspector will look for. Tucson has a hot desert climate, with average summer highs between 98 and 102 degrees and about 10.61 inches of rain a year.

The monsoon season officially starts June 15, and the first storms typically arrive around July 3 and can last into September. Roof flashing, stucco cracks, window seals and drainage around the foundation are the areas to check after one. The Santa Cruz River is dry much of the year but floods during heavy seasonal rain, so ask the city whether your parcel falls in a floodplain or wash zone before you set a price. The city's permit page notes that paving and grading in washes, hillside zones and floodplains always needs a permit.

Which permits come up when I sell a Tucson house?

Most residential work in Tucson needs a permit and inspection, and the city's Planning and Development Services Department (PDSD) runs the process through the Tucson Development Center Online portal. PDSD is in the Public Works Building at 201 N. Stone Avenue, and the phone is 520-791-5550.

The city says the owner is responsible for plans and a permit for:

  • New or replacement water heaters, furnaces, heat pumps and air conditioners, with load and sizing calculations for HVAC.
  • Electrical service increases and panel replacement or repair.
  • Detached accessory structures over 200 square feet, such as storage sheds.
  • Porches, additions, garages and remodels of existing structures.
  • Walls and fences, which need a zoning site plan review, and a building permit with engineered design above 7 feet.

Review time depends on the project. The Express Lane covers same-day items such as residential electrical and plumbing work. Fences and pools fall in the Fast Lane with a 15-day target, and alterations and new buildings sit in the Standard Lane with a 30-day goal. Interior finishes such as paint, carpet and cabinets need no permit, and a like-for-like toilet swap does not either.

What if work was done without a permit, or the utilities have been off?

You can still get a permit for finished work, but the same requirements apply. Tucson says you may obtain a permit for work that has already occurred, with a full set of construction drawings and completed inspections, and the owner should stop any ongoing work until the permit exists.

A vacant house raises a second issue. A permit is required to reconnect electric or gas service if the utility has been off to a residential structure for 6 consecutive months. The permit costs $135.59 and covers an inspection for obvious code or life-safety problems. Property in a Historic Preservation Zone, Neighborhood Preservation Zone or designated Historic Landmark needs a permit for any development, plus a design review.

Casitas are allowed in Tucson, one per residential lot, if they meet size and height standards. The city also treats rental units as commercial property, so commercial permits for them require a licensed contractor. Homeowners may use the owner-builder exemption under A.R.S. 32-1121 for their own residence, and the city warns it does not apply to any project that requires a building permit or where materials and labor exceed $1,000. Permit approval does not override any HOA covenants on the property.

How do Pima County property taxes work when I sell in Tucson?

The Pima County Treasurer bills and collects the tax on a Tucson house. Taxes above $100 are due in two installments. The first is due October 1 and becomes delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 1. The second is due March 1 and becomes delinquent after 5 p.m. on May 1.

For tax year 2026, the county lists the first-half deadline as a postmark no later than November 2, 2026, which has passed. The second-half postmark deadline is May 3, 2027. If the full year is paid before 5 p.m. on December 31, any interest on the first installment is waived. The Treasurer's number is 520-724-8341.

Ask your title company to order a payoff from the Treasurer so unpaid tax comes out of your proceeds at closing. To contest your value, the Pima County Assessor accepts a petition within 60 days of the postmark on a Notice of Value mailed on or before March 1.

What happens when the Tucson deed is recorded?

Documents that transfer real property go to the Pima County Recorder with a complete legal description and an Affidavit of Property Value under A.R.S. 11-1133. A deed submitted without a complete affidavit is rejected and returned.

If the transfer is exempt, the document must come with the Arizona Department of Revenue exemption letter and number. The recorder also requires an original signature, print no smaller than ten point, a page no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches and a 2-inch top margin on the first page. Since September 8, 2026, anyone presenting documents in person must show valid photo identification. The recorder does not give legal advice, so rely on your title company or attorney.

How long can a sale take in Tucson?

It depends on the route and on how clean the title is. A cash buyer can close on a date you choose once title work is clear, while a financed buyer adds appraisal and loan timelines. Ask your title company what it needs for a Pima County payoff and recording.

Do I need a permit to replace my water heater or air conditioner in Tucson?

Yes. Tucson requires a permit and inspection for new or replacement water heaters, and for new or replacement furnaces, heat pumps and air conditioners. HVAC permits need load and sizing calculations.

Can I sell a Tucson house that has unpermitted work?

You can sell it, but the work should be disclosed and ideally permitted first. Tucson allows permits for work already done if you supply full drawings and pass inspections. Ask PDSD at 520-791-5550 what applies to your address.

Who collects property tax on a Tucson house?

The Pima County Treasurer collects it. The Pima County Assessor sets the values. The first half becomes delinquent after November 1 and the second after May 1, with 2026 postmark deadlines of November 2, 2026 and May 3, 2027.

What is required to record a deed in Pima County?

A complete legal description and an Affidavit of Property Value, or an Arizona Department of Revenue exemption letter and number for an exempt transfer. In-person filers must show photo identification as of September 8, 2026.

Mesa stretches about 18 miles from Price Road in the west to Meridian Road in the east, and Center Street divides it into West Mesa and East Mesa for street numbering. The address tells a buyer at once which half of the city the house is in.

How did Mesa grow into a city of half a million?

Mesa grew from a Hohokam canal landscape and a Mormon farming settlement into a suburb that now holds more than 500,000 people. The Hohokam dug canals here at least 2,000 years ago, and the first Mesa company of settlers reused some of that canal work, with water flowing by April 1878. Mesa City was registered as a one-square-mile townsite on July 17, 1878, and incorporated in 1883 with about 300 residents.

Military airfields at Falcon Field and Williams Field in the early 1940s brought more people, and air conditioning and aerospace work pushed growth through the 1950s and 1960s. As late as 1960, half of Mesa's residents still earned a living from agriculture.

Wikipedia, citing the city's 2022 annual financial report, lists Mesa Public Schools (7,726 employees), Banner Health (6,826), Boeing (3,945) and the City of Mesa (3,579) as the largest local employers.

Main Street is the main east to west arterial, and Country Club Drive, Gilbert Road and Power Road carry traffic north and south.

Valley Metro light rail covers about four miles of Main Street, from Sycamore to Gilbert Road. Mesa Gateway Airport sits in the southeast corner, and the Polytechnic campus of Arizona State University is in southeast Mesa. Mesa Community College, which Wikipedia describes as the largest of the Maricopa Community Colleges, is also based here.

  • The rental unit needs a valid Arizona Transaction Privilege Tax license that lists its location.
  • Neighbors next to and surrounding the unit must be notified, with the Mesa license number, the address and an emergency contact.

How is a Mesa deed recorded at the Maricopa County Recorder?

The deed goes to the Maricopa County Recorder with an Affidavit of Property Value, or with an exemption code written on the document. Under A.R.S. 11-1133, the buyer and seller (or their agents) jointly certify the sale price, the parcel number, the date of sale, how the sale was financed and whether the home will be owner-occupied or rented. The recorder refuses a deed that lacks a complete affidavit unless it carries an exemption notation.

The standard fee is $30 per document, with some exceptions listed on the recorder's fee page. The office at 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200 in Phoenix is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., and the recorder says its staff cannot advise which code fits a deed. In practice a title or escrow company prepares and submits the package.

When are Mesa property taxes due, and how are they handled at closing?

Arizona property tax is paid in two halves, due October 1 and the following March 1. Under A.R.S. 42-18052, the first half goes delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and the second after 5:00 p.m. on May 1. A bill of $100 or less is due in full on October 1 and goes delinquent after December 31.

Gilbert is a town in Maricopa County, southeast of Phoenix, with 287,285 residents on July 1, 2025 according to the Census Bureau. It sits south of Mesa, northeast of Chandler and northwest of Queen Creek, and it covers about 68.6 square miles of land. Gilbert is legally a town even though it is larger than most Arizona cities.

The place began in 1902 when William "Bobby" Gilbert provided land to the Arizona Eastern Railway for a line between Phoenix and Florence. Ayer's Grocery opened in 1910, the post office followed in 1912, and Gilbert incorporated on July 6, 1920. Hay shipping gave it the nickname "Hay Capital of the World" from 1911 until the late 1920s, and the 1913 Gilbert Elementary School building now houses the Gilbert Historical Museum. The population was 29,188 in 1990, 208,453 in 2010 and 267,918 in 2020.

Most Gilbert addresses are zoned to Gilbert Public Schools, while other parts of town fall in the Chandler Unified, Mesa Public Schools or Higley Unified districts. You have 60 days from the date the Maricopa County Assessor mailed the Notice of Value. The petition goes to the Assessor first, and a denial can be taken to the State Board of Equalization within 25 days or to court by December 15.

Permits carry deadlines that matter when a seller is finishing a project. A value appeal begins with the Assessor. Notices of Value go out between January 1 and March 1, and a petition for review is due 60 days after the mailing date. A.R.S. 42-16051 requires the petition to state your opinion of full cash value with supporting information, such as the sale price of a comparable property. If the Assessor denies it, the next step is the State Board of Equalization, and the county's own materials say court filings are due by December 15. Because Arizona taxes the limited property value and that figure rises at most 5% a year, a lower full cash value helps only when it falls below the limited value.

Deeds for a Glendale sale are recorded by the Maricopa County Recorder, which handles more than 52 million documents and tells callers to use a title company or attorney for form questions. Yes, if tenants live there. Arizona law requires the owner of residential rental property to keep registration details on file with the county assessor and to update them within ten days of a change. Without that filing, a tenant can end the lease and recover prepaid rent.

Does Glendale charge city tax on long-term rental income?

No, not since January 1, 2025. The city says owners of residential rentals of 30 days or more no longer report or remit city transaction privilege tax on that income, though the property must still be registered with the county assessor.

The owner gives the city emergency and complaint contacts under City Code Section 29.1-41, holds a state transaction privilege tax license, and collects tax at a combined rate the city reports as 15.7%. A short-term rental is a residential property rented for fewer than 30 days.

The first half turns delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and the second half after 5:00 p.m. on May 1. For 2026 the county lists November 2 for the first half because November 1 fell on a Sunday.

A Glendale permit expires if work does not begin within 180 days, and one passed inspection is needed in every 180 day period. The project has a two year maximum, and an extension of an unexpired permit costs 50 percent of the original fee.

The area was farmed by the Hohokam, who dug canals there. Settlers later ran a ferry on the river, and Darrell Duppa suggested the name Tempe in 1879. Buyers ask about commutes first, so lead with these:

How does Tempe's desert heat affect the house I am selling?

The heat makes the cooling system the item buyers care about most. Tempe has a hot-desert climate, with average daily highs of 103.7 degrees in June, 105.9 in July and 104.8 in August, and a recorded high of 119. Yearly precipitation averages 8.80 inches.

A cooling unit that struggles in July is a bargaining point, and an old evaporative cooler or a roof with sun-cracked coating invites a repair credit request. If the unit is near the end of its life, get a written quote before you list so the number is yours and not the buyer's.

Rare storms do happen. An F2 tornado crossed Tempe on August 30, 1971 and injured 41 people. Check roof and window condition after any storm and keep the repair paperwork with your disclosure records.

Any work you did on the house should have its permits closed out before you list. The city's Building Safety Division is at 31 East 5th Street, Garden Level East, east of Mill Avenue between 5th and 6th Streets. Reach the permit center at PermitCenter@tempe.gov or 480-350-4311.

Residential plan review covers single-family homes, duplexes and townhomes. New construction, additions, renovations, remodels and accessory structures need plan approval before a permit is issued. The same staff answer accessory dwelling unit questions.

If a previous owner added a room, a carport or a casita, ask the division what is on record for your address. Learning that before a buyer's agent asks gives you time to finish or close a permit instead of negotiating around it.

Tempe's rental housing code sets standards that an inspecting buyer may notice. Landlords must provide:

  • Heating under the tenant's control that can bring habitable rooms to at least 70 degrees.
  • Cooling that holds rooms at 82 degrees or less with air conditioning, or 88 degrees or less with evaporative cooling.
  • Hot water at a minimum of 110 degrees.
  • Landscaping in yard areas visible to the public.

For short-term rentals, anyone renting a property for 29 days or less needs a Tempe Short-Term Rental License, one per unit. Owners must show $500,000 or more in liability coverage, notify adjacent neighbors and carry a state transaction privilege tax license. Maricopa County bills and collects the tax on a Tempe house, not the city. That date has passed, so confirm with the Treasurer whether yours is paid.

December 31, 2026 is the last day to pay current full-year taxes without interest on bills over $100. Under A.R.S. 42-18052 the second installment is due March 1 and becomes delinquent after May 1. On a closing, the escrow officer normally pays what is owed from your proceeds, so ask the title company to request a payoff from the Treasurer.

If you think the assessed value of your house is wrong, the Arizona Department of Revenue says a real property appeal goes to the County Assessor within 60 days of the Notice of Value. Appeals are about value and classification, and a high tax bill by itself is not a ground.

The deed is recorded with the Maricopa County Recorder at 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200, Phoenix, open Monday to Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. The standard recording fee is $30 per document, with some exceptions, and documents can be recorded in person, by mail or electronically.

Arizona law requires an Affidavit of Property Value with each deed, unless the transfer is exempt and the deed carries an exemption code. Under A.R.S. 11-1133 the buyer and seller, or their agents, certify the sale date, total price, financing type, parcel number and whether the house will be owner-occupied or rented. The recorder must refuse a deed that lacks a complete affidavit. The state notes that the sale date is the date the contract was signed, not the closing date. Your title company prepares and files this package, but read the affidavit before you sign it.

Contact the Building Safety Division at PermitCenter@tempe.gov or 480-350-4311. Staff can tell you what permits are on file, which matters if a prior owner built an addition or accessory structure.

What if I have not paid the first half of my 2026 Tempe property tax?

Pay it or ask your escrow officer to pay it from the sale. The first half became delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 2, 2026. The county calendar lists December 31 as the last day to pay current full-year taxes without interest.

What is Goodyear like, and how did it grow?

Goodyear is a city in Maricopa County about 17 miles west of downtown Phoenix, and its 191 square miles of land make it far larger than most neighbors. Avondale, Litchfield Park, Tolleson and Buckeye lie nearby, and the northern edge meets Glendale. The Gila River crosses the city, and the Estrella Mountains rise near its southern communities.

The Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company started the settlement in 1917 by buying 16,000 acres to grow cotton for tire cord. Goodyear became a town on November 19, 1946 and a city in 1985, and in 1987 the last 10,000 acres of company farmland were sold for future development. Most of the building happened after 1990. Estrella, south of the Gila River, is the largest master-planned community at about 20,000 acres, Palm Valley lies north of Interstate 10, and PebbleCreek is built for active adults. Goodyear Ballpark hosts spring training for the Cleveland Guardians and the Cincinnati Reds.

Because so many Goodyear homes sit inside planned communities, an HOA often shapes what a seller can do. The city's own code compliance page says some neighborhood rules, such as parking limits, come from private covenants enforced by an association instead of city code. Goodyear's Code Compliance Division responds to complaints about property that can be seen from the public right of way, so a seller should walk the front and sides of the house the way an inspector or neighbor would. Cases usually take 30 to 45 days to resolve, and a notice typically allows 10 to 30 days to fix a violation. The division can be reached at 623-882-7815 or codecompliance@goodyearaz.gov.

  • Weeds and grass on residential lots must stay under six inches and cannot hang over a sidewalk.
  • Recreational vehicles, boats and trailers belong in a garage or a paved side or rear yard behind a solid six foot fence, and no more than two may be stored there.

  • Front yard fences top out at three feet and rear yard fences at six feet, and fences under six feet generally need no building permit.
  • Trash and recycling containers stay out of view of the street except on collection days.

The city notes that violations on vacant and foreclosed homes can take months or longer to resolve because owners are hard to locate. If a Goodyear house sits empty, keep the yard cleared and a mailing address on file with the county so notices reach you.

Do Goodyear permits and building codes matter when selling?

Yes. Goodyear's homeowner guidance says all plan submittals and inspections must follow the adopted building codes, amendments and ordinances, including sound mitigation. Permitted work has to remain exposed for inspection, so ask the city whether past projects on the house, such as a pool, patio cover or addition, have a closed permit.

The city's EZ Permit lane covers minor jobs such as a residential pool or spa built from approved standard plans, and those permits are reviewed within five business days. Larger jobs, such as an addition or a detached accessory structure, go through the regular residential submittal guides on the Development Resources page. Questions go to the Building Safety Division at 623-932-3004 or buildingsafety@goodyearaz.gov. Check your HOA covenants as well, because the city says the owner, not the city, is responsible for knowing them before any modification.

A Goodyear owner who rents out the house must register it with the Maricopa County Assessor under A.R.S. 33-1902, and the city says failing to register carries a mandatory civil penalty of $1,000 plus $100 for each additional month. Goodyear also adopted a Residential Rental Property Ordinance, Article 11-1-21, that sets minimum health and safety standards for the interior and exterior of any apartment, single-family home or mobile home rented for a fee.

Short stays are handled separately. Goodyear's Finance Department runs a short-term rental licensing program with its own application requirements, listing requirements, annual renewal and an emergency and complaint contact record that owners keep current. The Finance Department's short-term rental desk is at 1900 N Civic Square, reachable at str@goodyearaz.gov or 623-882-7887 option 4. Yes, with a city license. Goodyear's Finance Department runs the licensing program, owners keep emergency and complaint contacts on file, and State law bars cities from prohibiting short-term rentals. Licensing questions go to str@goodyearaz.gov.

How many pets and recreational vehicles can I keep at a Goodyear house?

Goodyear limits households to four pets, and it lets a property store no more than two recreational vehicles, trailers or boats in the side or rear yard, on a paved surface behind a solid six foot fence.

Generally not for fences under six feet, but exceptions can apply. Front yard fences may reach three feet and rear yard fences six feet. Call the Development Counter at 623-932-3004 before building.

Half is due October 1 and half is due March 1. The first half turns delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and the second after 5:00 p.m. on May 1, with Maricopa County listing November 2 for 2026 because November 1 fell on a Sunday.

Sellers here include military households tied to Marine Corps Air Station Yuma and Yuma Proving Ground, and owners who live elsewhere for part of the year. What is Yuma like, and who buys houses here?

Yuma sits in the southwest corner of Arizona, just west of where the Gila River meets the Colorado River, with California to the west and Mexico to the south. The Colorado narrows to under 1,000 feet at the spot known as the Yuma Crossing, which made this a gateway for travelers heading to California during and after the Gold Rush.

Fort Yuma and a river crossing shaped the early town. A settlement called Arizona City took the name Yuma in 1873, Yuma became the county seat in 1871 after La Paz, and the Southern Pacific bridged the river in 1877. The Yuma Quartermaster Depot, established in 1864, supplied forts across the territory. The city incorporated in 1914.

The economy rests on agriculture and the military. Yuma County grows more than 175 crops, lettuce the largest, and provides 90% of the leafy vegetables grown in the United States from November to March. Marine Corps Air Station Yuma and the Army's Yuma Proving Ground are the other anchors.

Intense sun and long summers wear on roofs, coatings and cooling equipment, and buyers know it. Yuma is the driest and sunniest populated place in the contiguous United States, with 3.36 inches of rain in an average year.

In the 1991 to 2020 period, the temperature reached 100 degrees or higher on 117 days a year, mostly from April through October. The all-time high is 124 degrees, set in 1995. A roof, a cooling system and a water heater in their final years deserve a quote or an inspection before you list.

Applications can be filed through the city's Development Portal.

Arizona law requires a signed Affidavit of Property Value with the deed unless an exemption applies. The sale date is the date the contract was signed. Ask the Recorder's Office for the current fee schedule before you pay by mail.

Interest accrues at 16% a year, simple, prorated monthly. Delinquent taxes from 2025 take a 5% penalty on January 1, 2027, and unpaid parcels can be sold at the county tax lien sale on February 18, 2027.

Rentals in the city's revitalization areas are inspected under Chapter 138 of the Yuma Code of Ordinances. Inspectors need the tenant's signed access form, and the owner repairs any problems before certification.

Flagstaff began as a lumber and railroad town and later became a Route 66 stop. The first permanent settlement came in 1876, when Thomas F. McMillan built a cabin north of the present downtown, and a flagstaff was raised at the spring on July 4 of that year. The railroad arrived in the early 1880s, Coconino County was created in 1891 with Flagstaff as county seat, and Percival Lowell chose Flagstaff for his observatory in 1894. Education, health care, government and tourism drive Flagstaff, and each puts steady pressure on housing. Coconino County charges a flat $30 to record a document, and the fee includes the affidavit of property value and postage. The county adopted the flat fee on July 1, 2019, and it applies to deeds of conveyance as well as deeds of trust.

The recorder checks each document against the recording requirements in A.R.S. 11-480 and, if it is complete and the fee is paid, assigns a recording number. Mailed originals come back in about 4 to 6 weeks, while in-person documents are returned after scanning. Your escrow company usually handles recording on closing day.

Do I owe property tax if I sell in the middle of the year?

Ask your escrow officer how the year's tax will be split between you and the buyer. Mohave County bills are due October 1 and March 1, with the first half past due after November 1. The settlement statement should show the split.

Does Kingman allow short-term rentals?

Yes, with a permit. The city requires a permit, a Transaction Privilege Tax license, an emergency contact and neighbor notice for rentals under 30 days inside city limits. Arizona law at A.R.S. 9-500.39 limits how far a city may restrict them, but a permit is allowed. The city's rental page lists a $60 annual fee.

Start with a title company, because the recorder's staff cannot give legal advice or do research for you. The Mohave County Recorder at (928) 753-0701 can show you how to run a basic search by name, and a title company can tell you whether liens or judgments will cut into your proceeds.

Where is El Mirage, and what is the city like?

El Mirage is a small city in the northwest Phoenix area of Maricopa County, along the Agua Fria River and U.S. Route 60 (Grand Avenue). It covers 9.95 square miles, and the Census Bureau estimates 35,820 residents as of July 1, 2025. Downtown Phoenix is about 19 miles southeast by way of US 60.

El Mirage sits among several other communities:

  • Youngtown borders it to the east
  • Glendale borders it to the south
  • Surprise borders it to the northwest
  • Unincorporated Sun City lies to the northeast

Because the city is compact, a house in El Mirage is often described by the nearby cross streets and the school it feeds.

Households here are larger than in the other three cities compared in this guide. The Census Bureau counts 3.24 persons per household, and 27.7% of residents are under 18, compared with 22.8% in Chandler. Buyers shopping in El Mirage are frequently families looking for several bedrooms and a yard.

What is the history of El Mirage?

El Mirage grew out of Hohokam irrigation, 1930s farm labor and a long fight over land near Luke Air Force Base. The Hohokam, known as the Canal Builders, were the earliest inhabitants and built an irrigation network with stone tools and organized labor. In the early 1930s migrant farm workers settled on the west bank of the Agua Fria River, and Mexican migrants helped build canals and harvest the first crops.

The community became an incorporated town on June 25, 1951, and voters made it a city in a special election in 1983. In 1977 El Mirage annexed 2,000 acres for a planned community, and the state attorney general sued because the land lay close to Luke Air Force Base. The suit failed, but the base's objections later stopped the 1980s resort and convention center plan.

Growth came quickly in the 2000s: the 2000 census counted 7,609 people, the 2010 census 31,797 and the 2020 census 35,805. Farming remains part of the local story, and industrial growth has since added to it. The Historic Agua Fria River Bridge, built in 1895, is among the sites recorded as local historic structures.

It can, because El Mirage is near Luke Air Force Base, which is described as the largest fighter pilot training base in NATO. Aircraft noise and overflights are a normal topic for homes in the area, and a buyer may ask about them.

Arizona law gives governments a way to record that information. Under A.R.S. 28-8485, the state or the governing body of a political subdivision that operates an airport may designate an airport influence area, which is property exposed to aircraft noise and overflight, and must file a record of it with the county recorder. The record is meant to notify owners and potential purchasers. Ask your title company or the Maricopa County Recorder whether your parcel falls in any recorded area, and share the answer with the buyer.

What permits and rental registration matter before selling in El Mirage?

El Mirage requires a permit for new construction, some repairs and alterations, and remodeling, renovation or enlargement of a building. The city's Development Services department runs building safety and permitting, and its Permit Center says that since January 2, 2024 all plans must be submitted online through the ELM Online Permitting portal. The same department takes requests for building inspections.

If a previous owner finished a garage, a patio or a room addition, ask Development Services for the permit and inspection record before you accept an offer. Planning and Zoning also maintains the General Plan and a zoning ordinance update, which a buyer planning an addition may want to read.

For houses that have been rented, Maricopa County's assessor shows the parcel type as Residential/Rental when a rental registration is on file. Ask the City of El Mirage Development Services whether a rental license or short-term rental registration applies to your address.

An El Mirage sale is recorded with the Maricopa County Recorder, which charges $30 for most documents. It records in person or by mail at 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200, Phoenix, and mailed originals come back in two to four weeks.

The affidavit rule is A.R.S. 11-1133, which requires price, sale date, legal description and parcel information. A.R.S. 11-1134 exempts certain transfers, such as a deed of gift, a quitclaim executed for no money, a court-ordered conveyance, and a nominal-consideration transfer between parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, siblings or spouses. Families settling a house after a death often fall into those categories, and an attorney or title officer can confirm which one fits.

Arizona property tax is payable in two halves, due October 1 and March 1. The Maricopa County Recorder charges $30 per document for deeds and most other filings. A deed also needs an affidavit of property value or an exemption code before it is accepted.

The median value is lower than the $471,300 reported for Goodyear and the $575,100 reported for Gilbert, so compare your own sale price and repair estimates before choosing a route.

What is Florence, Arizona like, and what shaped it?

Florence is the county seat of Pinal County, on the south bank of the Gila River at an elevation of about 1,539 feet. The Census Bureau estimates 25,222 residents as of July 1, 2025 and about 62.6 square miles of land, up from 52.5 square miles in 2010. State Routes 79 and 287 serve the town.

Levi Ruggles surveyed the townsite in the 1860s and secured a post office in 1866. Silver found in 1875 led to the Silver King Mine, and canals dug in the 1880s let farming and ranching grow. The town includes a National Historic District with more than 25 buildings on the National Register of Historic Places, the original Main Street townsite was listed on October 26, 1982, and Florence High School, built in 1887, is listed as well. The Territorial Prison opened in 1909 after the Yuma prison closed, and the town now hosts several state, federal, county and private prisons.

The Census count shows 6,719 households averaging 2.39 people, which comes to roughly 16,000 residents, while the headline population is 25,222. For a seller, the household count is the better guide to how many homes compete for buyers. Newer development has arrived too, including an Anthem community by Pulte and Del Webb about six miles northwest of the old townsite. The climate is lower Sonoran Desert, with a monsoon season that brings flash flood risk and afternoon thunderstorms, and winter storms that supply the other half of annual rain.

How does the Florence Historic District affect a house sale?

The Town also runs events such as a Walking Tour and a Historic District Home Tour. If you own an older house in town, ask the Town's Community Development Department two questions before listing: whether the property is in the district, and whether any planned repair, such as new windows or a new porch, triggers a compliance step.

When are Pinal County property taxes due for a Florence home?

Pinal County bills Florence property in two halves, with the first due October 1 and the second due March 1. Under the Treasurer's schedule the first half turns delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 1, and the second half after 5 p.m. on May 1. Because November 1, 2026 fell on a Sunday, the deadline moved to the next business day, and that date has passed. A bill of $100 or less is due October 1 in full.

Tell the escrow officer your tax status when you open escrow so the closing statement splits the year correctly. The Treasurer's main office is in Florence, and the Assessor keeps offices in Florence, Apache Junction, Casa Grande, Maricopa and San Tan Valley.

How do you appeal a Florence property valuation?

You appeal by filing a petition for review with the Pinal County Assessor within 60 days of the date the Notice of Value was mailed, and filing is free. Only the full cash value can be appealed, because taxes rest on the limited property value, which in most cases cannot rise more than 5% a year. If the limited value already sits below the market value you believe is right, a win will not lower the tax. After an Assessor denial, a second level is available at the Pinal County Board of Equalization within 25 days, and a further appeal can go to court within 60 days of the last decision. Taxes on a parcel in a court appeal must be paid before they become delinquent, or the court dismisses the case.

The deed for a Florence sale is recorded at the Pinal County Recorder's Office, 31 N Pinal Street, Building E, Florence. The phone is 520-866-6830. Documents can be recorded in person, by mail or through the county's approved electronic recording partners, and most sales reach the recorder through the title company.

  • Copies of recorded documents cost $1 per page, with $3 more for certification.
  • The Assessor's Parcel Alert List sends a free notice when a new deed is received for your parcel, a guard against deed fraud.

Landlords should confirm the house is registered with the Pinal County Assessor, since the Town of Florence states that all Arizona counties require residential rental registration. A.R.S. 33-1902 backs this up by barring occupancy of unregistered rental property and requiring updates within ten days of a change.

Short-term rentals of 29 days or less fall under the state's transient lodging classification and the Town's hotel classification for transaction privilege tax. Hosts should settle any back filings before they close, because underreported tax can bring interest and penalties.

The first half goes delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 1 and the second half after 5 p.m. on May 1. Late payments accrue 16% interest a year, prorated monthly, and interest cannot be waived.

You have 60 days from the mailing date of the Notice of Value to file a petition with the Pinal County Assessor. There is no filing fee, and the Assessor must rule by August 15.

Yes. Florence has a National Historic District with more than 25 buildings on the National Register of Historic Places, and the Town's preservation staff and Historic District Advisory Commission work with homeowners on compliance procedures and rehabilitation standards.
